newsitem.title: USA: Flamboyant McDougal helped Clinton's rise.
newsitem.headline: Flamboyant McDougal helped Clinton's rise.

text.p: James McDougal, who was sentenced to three years in prison on Monday, played a key role in Bill Clinton's political rise but then gave evidence against his former friend when facing hefty jail time for fraud.

McDougal, the central figure in the politically charged Whitewater investigation, was a flamboyant businessman and political player inside Arkansas when he took Clinton under his wing as the future president made his way up the Democratic Party ladder.
Apart from supporting him politically, McDougal, 56, also tried to ease Clinton's early financial difficulties by bringing him in on lucrative real estate ventures.

One of them brought Clinton a handy profit but the 230-acre (93 hectares) Whitewater residential project in northern Arkansas was a flop as the property market slumped and he could not sell the plots.
The failure strained their relationship during the 1980s and relations deteriorated when the Whitewater controversy flared within months of Clinton taking office in 1993.

McDougal and his Madison Guaranty Savings & Loan was at the heart of the Whitewater investigation from the very beginning. His thrift collapsed in 1989 at a cost of over $60 million to taxpayers and his cavalier business practices came under the close scrutiny of government regulators.

McDougal at first claimed he was the victim of a political attack on Clinton but when a federal jury found him guilty on 18 counts of fraud and conspiracy last May, he decided to cooperate with the same prosecutors he had slammed as "Republican henchmen".

Over the last nine months, McDougal has met regularly with Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr and reportedly corroborated allegations that Clinton pressured an Arkansas banker to extend an illegal $300,000 loan to McDougal's former wife Susan McDougal in 1986.

When McDougal was reminded on Monday that he had repeatedly predicted both the president and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton would be vindicated in the Whitewater probe, McDougal changed his tune: "I wouldn't go to the bank on that," he told reporters.
Clinton has flatly denied the allegations against him.
Starr said McDougal provided strong new information on the probe into Clinton's finances that was previously known only to a very small group of people.

That commendation helped persuade U.S. District Judge George Howard to sentence McDougal to just three years in prison and three years probation instead of a maximum 81-year prison sentence and $4.5 million fine he could have handed down.

McDougal was born and brought up in rural Arkansas but claims a Scottish lord among his ancestors and, even as a young man, stood apart from the crowd with his fierce intellect and taste for fast cars and expensive suits.

At his peak, McDougal was a prominent figure in Arkansas' business and political circles but his wealth and reputation collapsed as he overstretched himself financially and used fraudulent loans to help finance his ambitious plans.
The turning point for McDougal came in the mid-1980s as his marriage fell apart, he suffered a stroke and manic depression and then had his savings and loan closed down.
After his sentencing on Monday, McDougal denied lying in order to win leniency.

"I am not peddling the truth or asking people to believe anything. I have simply responded and I think that the documentary evidence will substantiate anything I have said to the independent counsel," he said.
